Apply a Thread Count for the Duration of One Fit

Source: R/threads.R
local_threads.Rd

Validates a threads argument and sets RcppParallel's thread count to it for the calling frame's lifetime, restoring the previous process state when that frame exits. An entry point such as statmodels7::statmod() or distributions7::fit_distrib() calls it once at the start of a fit; the count itself still travels to each kernel as an argument, and this call only sizes the worker pool from which the parallel regions draw.

Usage

local_threads(threads = 1, frame = parent.frame())

Arguments

threads

A single whole number, at least 1, and the default is 1. The count is passed to the compiled kernels unchanged, and a kernel still runs sequentially on an input below its internal threshold. Any other value signals an error: a value below 1, a fractional value, Inf, NA, a character string and a vector of length other than one are all rejected with the same message.

frame

The environment whose exit restores the previous setting, defaulting to the caller's. Pass an outer frame to hold the setting for longer than one call.

Value

The thread count, invisibly: a single integer, at least 1.

Threads and cores

threads is multithreading inside one R process: the compiled per-observation kernels and the dense assembly products run on several threads that share memory. It is distinct from cores, the argument of the functions that distribute independent fits over separate R processes (the folds of a cross-validation, the replicates of a bootstrap, the starts of optimizers7::multistart()). The two counts are independent, except that a fit running inside a separate R process is sequential by construction, so cores = 4 opens up to four processes and each of them fits on one thread; it never opens 4 * threads of them.

Results independent of the thread count

Every parallel region in the toolkit decomposes its work over the elements of its output. Each accumulated value is therefore summed in full by one thread, reductions are never split across threads, and a kernel returns the same bits at any count.

This holds because of two properties of the drivers, and not of the kernels. A worker installs the calling thread's floating-point environment before running its chunk, because without it some of the platform's own math routines (among them R's psigamma at higher orders, bessel_k, and pgamma and pbeta on the log scale) can return results that differ in the last bits between threads. The sequential branch also runs through the same compiled function as the parallel one, so a compiler cannot optimize the two differently.

The dense assembly products of statmodels7 are an exception. There, a count above 1 replaces a BLAS expression by a threaded kernel, which is a second implementation of the same sum. Its result is bit-exact against the reference BLAS shipped with R, and agrees within the rounding of one dot product with an optimized BLAS such as OpenBLAS or Accelerate, which accumulates in its own order.

The guarantee is a design constraint on any kernel added later.

The sequential path

At threads = 1 the code enters no parallel region and leaves the process-level thread setting unchanged. The code taken is the sequential one, not a parallel path running on a single thread.

Each kernel carries an internal threshold as well, measured where the cost of opening a parallel region overtakes its gain. Below it the kernel stays sequential regardless of the count.

Restoration

RcppParallel::setThreadOptions() writes a process-level variable, so a fit that set it and returned would leave it moved for whatever runs next. The restoration is therefore registered with on.exit in the caller's frame, which runs however the fit exits, also on an error.

Examples

f <- function() {
  local_threads(2)
  Sys.getenv("RCPP_PARALLEL_NUM_THREADS")
}
f()                                     # "2" inside the frame
#> [1] "2"
Sys.getenv("RCPP_PARALLEL_NUM_THREADS", unset = "unset")   # restored
#> [1] "unset"

# A count must be a single whole number of at least one.
try(local_threads(0))
#> Error : 'threads' must be a single whole number, at least 1.
try(local_threads(2.5))
#> Error : 'threads' must be a single whole number, at least 1.
